mcqs.question: What is the core argument for writing a design doc before implementing a risky change?
options: It satisfies a process requirement that most teams mandate
It moves disagreements to a stage where they're cheap to resolve, before code is written
It gives managers visibility into what engineers are working on
It's required so the change can be added to a roadmap
mcqs.explanation: The real value is economic: a disagreement caught in a paragraph costs a comment thread, while the same disagreement caught after implementation costs a rewrite. Process compliance, manager visibility, and roadmap tracking might be side effects, but they're not why the doc actually helps.

mcqs.question: A design doc for a new rate limiter lists "per-user limiting" as a non-goal. What is that non-goal actually doing?
options: Admitting the design has a flaw that needs to be fixed later
Pre-empting a legitimate but out-of-scope question so it doesn't derail the review
Listing a feature that was already rejected by leadership
Describing something the design accidentally breaks
mcqs.explanation: A non-goal scopes out a real, valid idea on purpose so reviewers don't spend the review debating it — it's a scoping tool, not an admission of failure or a record of a rejected feature, and it isn't about something broken by the design.

mcqs.question: Why does a strong alternatives section reject each option with a specific, concrete reason instead of a general one like "it seemed more complex"?
options: Because a concrete reason is shorter to write
Because reviewers are required to approve any option with a listed downside
Because a vague rejection can't be productively argued with, while a concrete one lets a reviewer actually disagree with the reasoning
Because listing more detail makes the document look more thorough
mcqs.explanation: The point of naming a real cost — an operations burden, a coupling risk, a concrete number — is that it's falsifiable: a reviewer can push back on the actual reasoning. A vague dismissal gives them nothing to engage with, which is the opposite of what an alternatives section is for.

mcqs.question: A team lead writes a doc for a decision they've already fully made, using the standard design-doc template with an honest-looking alternatives section. What's the actual problem here?
options: Using a design-doc template for an already-made decision is never appropriate
The alternatives section format is wrong for a settled decision
Nothing, as long as the reasoning in the doc is sound
Doing this silently wastes reviewer effort on alternatives that were never going to change anything, eroding trust in future docs
mcqs.explanation: The core issue isn't the format — it's presenting a settled decision as open for input without saying so. Reviewers who invest real effort proposing alternatives to a doc that can't change learn not to bother next time; an ADR-style doc that's honest about being a record avoids this entirely.

mcqs.question: A design doc has a solid problem statement, honest alternatives, and clear trade-offs, but implementation starts without anyone being sure review actually concluded. What's missing?
options: A diagram showing the system architecture
An explicit statement of what decision is being asked for and by when
A longer alternatives section
A non-goals section
mcqs.explanation: This is the "buried ask" failure applied to design docs specifically: without a stated decision deadline and a clear definition of what approval means, reviewers comment on sections but no one ever declares the doc approved. A diagram or a longer alternatives section doesn't fix an absent, explicit ask.

mcqs.question: What's the right heuristic for deciding whether a change needs the full design-doc treatment versus a short message?
options: How many engineers will be involved in building it
How long the implementation is expected to take
Whether the change is reversible and what the blast radius is if the decision turns out to be wrong
Whether the change touches more than one service
mcqs.explanation: The heuristic is cost-of-being-wrong, not size of the team or the codebase footprint — a small, easily reversible change across two services doesn't need a full doc, while a hard-to-reverse single-service schema migration does. Team size and service count are proxies that can mislead in either direction.
